title: Operating systems for good product work

questions.question: Monitoring detects a 34% rise in response time on day two. It reaches no decision forum for six weeks. Nobody was careless. Which stage of information flow failed hardest, and why?
options: Detection — the monitoring threshold was clearly set too loosely
Routing and standing — nobody owned carrying a monitoring signal into a product decision, and a problem with no complainant loses every prioritization contest
Cadence — the review meeting simply did not happen often enough
Artifact quality — the dashboard did not explain the business impact
questions.explanation: Detection worked; the number was visible the whole time. C is the tempting answer because adding a meeting is the reflex fix, but a faster meeting fed by tickets would still never have seen this signal. The absence of tickets is a fact about the channel before it is a fact about the world.

questions.question: A team reviews a metric weekly. The metric only moves meaningfully over about a month. What does this cadence produce?
options: Early warning, which is worth the extra meetings
Nothing much either way, since a short meeting is cheap
Thrash — the team reacts to variance and calls it learning
Better data quality, because the numbers get checked more often
questions.explanation: A decision cadence faster than the evidence cadence generates responses to noise. A is what a competent PM says, and early warning is a genuine goal — but you cannot get it from a metric that has not moved yet, only from a trigger on a leading observation.

questions.question: A leader finds that every significant trade-off escalates to them. They propose adding a weekly cross-functional prioritization forum. What is wrong with this?
options: The forum should be fortnightly to reduce overhead
Nothing — a forum is exactly how escalations get distributed
The forum needs a clearer pre-read artifact to be effective
An operating system cannot fix a direction or decision-rights problem; the escalation will simply become better attended
questions.explanation: This is the boundary of the model. If nothing in the direction orders the competing values, and no rights map assigns the residue, a new room gives the same escalation a slide and six people's time. C is tempting because pre-reads genuinely improve forums, and it would improve this one — while leaving the underlying cause untouched.

questions.question: Which recurring meeting should be first in line for removal?
options: The well-attended weekly review that everyone finds useful but which disposed of no decision last month
The sparsely attended monthly forum where two capacity decisions were made
The quarterly retro, because retros rarely change anything
The engineering-only technical review, since the PM is not present
questions.explanation: The audit question is what was decided, not who came or how it felt. A is uncomfortable precisely because attendance and satisfaction are high — which is why it survives every review. B passes the test despite poor attendance. If A has real value as shared context, keep it and label it as such; do not count it as decision infrastructure.

questions.question: A team runs a quarterly planning forum. A core dependency loses vendor support in ten weeks. What does the cadence rule require?
options: Move the whole planning forum to a six-week cycle
Give this decision a trigger rather than a calendar slot, because the consequence closes faster than the loop runs
Raise it at the next quarterly forum with a higher priority score
Delegate the decision to engineering so the forum is not needed
questions.explanation: Cadence answers to two constraints, and when the consequence clock is shorter than the loop, the consequence wins. A over-corrects the entire system for one decision and imposes the cost on everything else. C is the answer that loses the option: by the next quarterly forum, part of the ten weeks is already spent.
